plot: A hardworking fisherman and his wife in early 20th century Korea take in lodgers for extra income while their son Hoonie, born with physical differences but intelligent, comes of age during the Japanese annexation of Korea in 1910.

A man's engagement falls apart after his fiancée, a "bad-ass salcedense" who had explicitly warned against infidelity, discovers he's been unfaithful with fifty women over six years, leading to a painful six-month period where their relationship slowly unravels despite their history together.

A Native American elder named Nanapush recounts how his Anishinabe people were devastated by successive waves of disease, forced relocation, and government treaties, leaving him as the last of his family and one of the few survivors who witnessed the end of their traditional way of life.

A female writer meets with a billionaire at a London club to discuss a potential literary magazine, but instead the billionaire  discusses his various ambitious projects and personal life before sending her off in a taxi to catch a flight to Athens, a destination she doesn't recall mentioning.

A man reflects on the profound intimacy and security he found with Catherine, contrasting their rare connection where they could be "alone together" against the world's inevitable breaking of the human spirit.

The narrator, who became a novelist at age 22, gave his first completed novel to his father 23 years before inheriting his suitcase, and his father's emotional embrace and encouraging prediction that he would one day win a prestigious literary prize (which he eventually did) remained a source of support until his father's death in 2002.

The narrator, who privately dubbed their mother's younger cousin Ernie Botts as "Earnest Bottom," receives regular dinner invitations from this well-groomed bachelor after moving to his city for college, continuing a familial connection despite their seeming lack of compatibility.

A dystopian scenario where the narrator recalls yearning for an undefined future while being held in a monitored dormitory facility with restricted movement, experiencing isolation under the surveillance of female authority figures Aunt Sara and Elizabeth and guards called Angels, whom they simultaneously fear yet fantasize about communicating in exchange of sex as potential means of escape or human connection.

voice: third person with brief dialogue in first person
plot: Marianne and Connell share an intimate moment as they discuss Connell's potential move to New York, reflecting on their deep connection, how they've shaped each other's lives, and the bittersweet understanding that their relationship may be changing forever.

A young narrator in an upscale Tours restaurant painfully observes the stark contrast between herself and her father's awkward, neglected experience and a confident teenage girl dining nearby, later decoding that her father's persistent complaints about "pig slop" mashed potatoes masked his resentment at their treatment as unsophisticated customers.

A daughter watches their mother during her final day of life that coincides with St Patricks Day in a Duluth hospital, observing her persistently open blue eyes as she transitions from life to death with a fierce desire to remain alive.

An elderly man named Junior falls down on a day that begins like any other, with vivid sensory details of daily life in Chennai near Elliot's Beach, as he and another old man named Senior emerge onto their adjacent verandas at the same moment, seemingly caught in a moment of fateful coincidence.

In a once-European resort town in Africa, abandoned colonial buildings have been repurposed by Africans from the forest, who adapted the angular structures to their traditional living patterns, while remnants of European life lie discarded amidst encroaching nature, signaling the town's loss of purpose following independence, political upheaval, and the exodus of white and Asian populations.

A young adult declines joining their father, stepmother Chitra, and half-sisters Rupa and Piu on a Disney World trip, preferring solitude at home while grappling with family dynamics and the memory of their deceased mother.

A person stands in Norfolk contemplating debris in an empty field and briefly imagines it as a collection of all their lost things, allowing themselves a fleeting fantasy that their recently deceased loved one Tommy might appear in the distance, before returning to their car.

voice: third person with majority of it as dialogue in first person
plot: Samad laments to an unnamed friend that immigration to England has left him feeling trapped between cultures, with one son becoming too English and the other too religious, while expressing his profound disillusionment with life in England and questioning whether belonging anywhere is even possible.

A woman dining with her partner Jean-Marc experiences a paradoxical moment of nostalgia for him despite his presence, connects this feeling to memories of her dead child, and experiences an uncensored wave of happiness that later frightens her.

A person becomes obsessed with cooking and eating spaghetti alone during what they call "the Year of Spaghetti" in 1971 AD, gathering specialized equipment, cookbooks  and transforming their apartment into a pasta laboratory filled with exotic ingredients and aromas.

A  young mother, alone and afraid, delivers her own baby, sews a tiny gown, and desperately prays for the child's survival, only to have the infant die in her arms an hour later after briefly opening its eyes.

A man glimpses a strikingly beautiful woman at Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris, is instantly captivated by her before she disappears into the crowd, and when later questioned by a ticket clerk about his distraction, he asks if she believes in love at first sight.

A writer named Briony reveals they changed their story's ending to allow the real life lovers Robbie Turner and Cecilia to survive and reunite, rather than maintaining the tragic historical truth that both died during World War II.

A man who previously assassinated a premier contemplates killing another political leader, torn between the desire to create a movement for justice and the option of returning to his former life of anonymity, ultimately deciding to move forward with the attack.

A daughter visits her elderly father who appears to be experiencing cognitive decline, struggling to remember his current work and expressing distress over his inability to connect with her, while her mother attempts to manage the situation and later laments his aging by showing a photo from his vibrant academic past.

A grieving narrator confronts a significant milestone in mourning when they realize their mental timeline of memories has reached the point where their deceased husband John was no longer alive on the previous year's corresponding date, highlighting the tension between preserving his memory and accepting the need to move forward with life.

Quentin contemplates the passage of time as he observes shadows on the curtains and reflects on his grandfather's pocket watch, which his father gave him with philosophical musings about the futility of humanity's struggle against time and the illusion of victory.

Dr. John Montague, a scholarly doctor of philosophy in anthropology seeking validation, rents the ominous and isolated Hill House for three months to investigate supernatural phenomena and document psychic disturbances, hoping to make his reputation with a definitive work on this notoriously haunted dwelling.

Dana, a time traveler, reflects on how disturbingly easy it's been for her and Kevin to adapt to living in a slaveholder's household, feeling moral discomfort about her relationship with her master while Kevin romanticizes staying to witness history despite her objections about the treatment of Black people and Native Americans.

A woman watches footage of 9/11 repeatedly, particularly focusing on a falling woman who reminds her of her friend Reva, who was lost in the attacks, finding a disturbing beauty in the image that makes her feel alive.

Orin suffers from intense morning anxiety after nightmares about spiders and heights, which is made worse when he wakes up with a sexual partner still present, leaving him feeling that the day ahead must be climbed vertically like a cliff rather than simply traversed.

A desolate journey through a charred wasteland that leads to an impassable swamp, where a traveler encounters a blind man walking toward the desolation, prompting concern about whether the blind man knows the road's futile destination.

The Misfit, a troubled man, engages in a brief moment of human connection with an elderly grandmother before violently shooting her, then reflects that she might have been a good person if continually faced with death.

Argue how "home" is not a physical place you can leave behind, but rather an internal, youthful region carried within us throughout life—where our true, childlike selves reside as the only real inhabitants, serving as our safest and most authentic place of belonging.

The narrator is planning to secretly assist her terminally ill friend with their chosen end-of-life plan, which involves leaving for an undetermined period and maintaining complete secrecy about their intentions, as the friend has decided to end her life naturally after stopping chemotherapy and wants peace without intervention during her final days.

A climactic confrontation between gay cowboys Jack and Ennis where Jack emotionally expresses his frustration about their limited, secretive relationship spanning twenty years, culminating in Ennis's physical collapse and their ultimate return to an unresolved status quo.

Kant, a 31-year-old video game designer, comes out as gay through a mass email after years of anxiety and self-denial, only to receive universal support that leaves him paradoxically adrift and unchanged in his habits.

Mrs. Dalloway sets out to buy flowers on a beautiful morning while preparing for a party, which triggers vivid memories of her youth at Bourton where she experienced both exhilaration and solemnity, and recalls Peter Walsh's memorable quip about preferring men to vegetables as she anticipates his imminent return from India.

A person experiences a profound moment of transcendence while gazing at Manhattan's skyline at night, feeling their individual identity dissolve into a larger sense of abstract collective potential that connects them to both the urban landscape and a loved one named Noor, while contemplating how present experiences might be reinterpreted in the future.

The Jewish community of Newark during World War II found escape and pride through idolizing Seymour "Swede" Levov, an anomalous blond, blue-eyed Jewish high school sports star who allowed them to temporarily forget their academic focus, the war's harsh realities, and their fears for loved ones serving overseas.

A 38-year-old pregnant woman discovers her husband's affair with an unattractive woman named Thelma Rice through an inscription in a book of children's songs, flees to her father's  depressing apartment in New York, and attempts to cope with her heartbreak through humor.

A craftsman who made a special bag for a patient rides an elevator to the sixth floor of a hospital in a disturbing scenario, planning to apologize and manipulate her into wearing the bag one last time before her surgery, then violently attack her with hidden shears to cut out her heart out.

A woman grappling with perceived contradictions between her feminist beliefs and her personal desires, including wanting both independence and care, enjoying traditionally feminine things while feeling they compromise her feminist identity, and struggling with how to reconcile these conflicting aspects of herself.

In a moment of unexpected joy, Holden Caulfield stands soaking wet in the rain watching his sister Phoebe ride a carousel, feeling deeply happy despite his usual cynicism, then shifts to discuss his hospitalization, deflecting questions about applying himself at his new school in the fall, expressing uncertainty about his future, mentioning visits from his brother D.B. and his attractive English girlfriend, and concluding with the melancholic realization that after telling his story, he misses everyone he's mentioned—even those he claimed to dislike

A writer describes their personal struggle with racial identity, having faced criticism from Black and white people alike for not being "Black enough" in both personal interactions and their literary work, which focuses on classical retellings and poststructuralist parodies rather than stereotypical "authentic" Black narratives that publishers and agents believe would sell better, ultimately concluding that while they rarely think about race and don't believe in it as a concept, they acknowledge its real-world consequences through discrimination based on physical attributes and ancestry.

A wounded and terrified woman named Wendy desperately flees up a staircase and down a hallway from a bloodied man named Jack who pursues her with a roque mallet, threatening to bash her brains in amid bizarre hallucinations of a masked party-goer, and despite both their injuries, she narrowly avoids being struck when Jack falls.

The narrator, left alone after Sylvie's silent departure without warning, contemplates creating an ice statue of a woman by a frozen pond or path in the woods that would stand as a beautiful maternal figure by the water, who, unlike the biblical barren salt pillar of Lot's wife who was punished for looking back in mourning, would be adorned with flowers and surrounded by children who would admire, love, and forgive her for turning away despite her stillness and icy hands.

A journalist and his attorney frantically acquire drugs, rent a powerful convertible, and attempt to purchase high-end Belgian Heliowatt audio equipment with a voice-activated shotgun microphone in Hollywood on a Friday afternoon, encountering various obstacles including a fatal pedestrian accident on Sunset Boulevard and hostile salesmen who reluctantly sell them equipment through a barely-opened door while brandishing tire irons, all in preparation for a chaotic drug-fueled road trip from Los Angeles to Las Vegas

Walter and Patty Berglund, once respected urban pioneers who renovated a Victorian home in a declining St. Paul neighborhood where they faced challenges (including vandalism and intimidating neighbors), have fallen from grace after moving to Washington D.C., with Walter becoming embroiled in a professional scandal involving the coal industry that contradicts his formerly eco-friendly reputation and surprises their former neighbors, while highlighting how Patty was notably visible as a young mother determinedly navigating urban difficulties.

A tense dinner party scene where the protagonist Ifemelu boldly speaks truth about the unspoken racial dynamics in interracial relationships in America despite polite social pretenses in front of her partner Blaine, causing discomfort among the liberal guests, and then begins to share her personal experience with her white ex-boyfriend Curt.

A person grappling with the contradiction of creating a refuge for Black people (Valentine Farm) within a nation built on injustice, while also questioning how to represent the diverse needs and identities of African Americans who share oppression but come from varied cultural backgrounds.

A person  takes a temporary Christmas job as a mail carrier, meets a lonely married woman while delivering mail, has a brief sexual relationship with her only to lose interest a few days later, and realizes that being a mailman might be an ideal job due to the perceived opportunity for casual sexual encounters.
